idea.before:
The definition is a guarantee in two parts. Accuracy $\varepsilon$ says how close to perfect the output must be (an approximately correct predictor); confidence $\delta$ says how often the sample may be so unlucky that it fails (probably). The quantifier order carries the content: $m_{\mathcal H}$ is fixed first and must then work against an adversary who picks the worst $\mathcal D$ and $f$ afterwards, which is what makes the guarantee distribution-free. For axis-aligned rectangles the tightest-box learner of ml-2.1e's setting is PAC with $m_{\mathcal H}(\varepsilon,\delta)=\lceil\ln(4/\delta)/\ln(1/(1-\varepsilon/4))\rceil\approx4\ln(4/\delta)/\varepsilon$, since the error region is covered by four strips each of mass $\varepsilon/4$ and each is missed by all $m$ examples with probability $(1-\varepsilon/4)^m$.

Starting from the stated four-strip failure bound, put $q=1-\varepsilon/4\in(0,1)$. The exponential and logarithm properties (pma 8.6) give $q^m=e^{-m\log(1/q)}$ with $\log(1/q)>0$. Therefore $4q^m\le\delta$ is equivalent to $m\ge\log(4/\delta)/\log(1/q)$, explaining the ceiling and the positive denominator in the sample size. This algebra converts the geometric bound; it does not supply the strip argument itself.
idea.after:
The definition is a guarantee in two parts. Accuracy $\varepsilon$ says how close to perfect the output must be (an approximately correct predictor); confidence $\delta$ says how often the sample may be so unlucky that it fails (probably). The quantifier order carries the content: $m_{\mathcal H}$ is fixed first and must then work against an adversary who picks the worst $\mathcal D$ and $f$ afterwards, which is what makes the guarantee distribution-free. For axis-aligned rectangles the tightest-box learner of ml-2.1e's setting is PAC with $m_{\mathcal H}(\varepsilon,\delta)=\lceil\ln(4/\delta)/\ln(1/(1-\varepsilon/4))\rceil\approx4\ln(4/\delta)/\varepsilon$. For the strip argument put $q=\varepsilon/4$ and restrict the measure to the target rectangle $R$. If $\mathcal D(R)\le q$, a missed side of mass greater than $q$ is impossible. Otherwise fix, for each of the four oriented coordinates, the first cumulative-mass quantile reaching $q$, including its boundary atom in a witness strip. Its mass is at least $q$. Any strict missed-side strip of mass greater than $q$ contains that fixed witness; the cutoff depends on $R$ and the law, not on the sample. If total missed mass exceeds $\varepsilon$, one of the four sides exceeds $q$, so every example misses its witness. If there are no positive examples, all witnesses are missed. Each such miss event has probability at most $(1-q)^m$, giving the four-event union bound. Atomless laws permit exact-mass strips; atoms may increase a witness's mass and only improve its miss bound.

Starting from the stated four-strip failure bound, put $q=1-\varepsilon/4\in(0,1)$. The exponential and logarithm properties (pma 8.6) give $q^m=e^{-m\log(1/q)}$ with $\log(1/q)>0$. Therefore $4q^m\le\delta$ is equivalent to $m\ge\log(4/\delta)/\log(1/q)$, explaining the ceiling and the positive denominator in the sample size. This algebra converts the geometric bound; it does not supply the strip argument itself.

statement.before:
Let $\theta_1,\dots,\theta_m$ be i.i.d. random variables with $\mathbb E[\theta_i]=\mu$ and $\mathbb P[a\le\theta_i\le b]=1$. Then for every $\varepsilon>0$
$$\mathbb P\Big[\Big|\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i-\mu\Big|>\varepsilon\Big]\;\le\;2\exp\!\Big(-\frac{2m\varepsilon^2}{(b-a)^2}\Big).$$
statement.after:
Let $\theta_1,\dots,\theta_m$ be i.i.d. random variables with $\mathbb E[\theta_i]=\mu$ and $\mathbb P[a\le\theta_i\le b]=1$ with $a<b$. Then for every $\varepsilon>0$
$$\mathbb P\Big[\Big|\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i-\mu\Big|>\varepsilon\Big]\;\le\;2\exp\!\Big(-\frac{2m\varepsilon^2}{(b-a)^2}\Big).$$ If $a=b$, every variable equals that constant almost surely, so the displayed deviation event has probability zero for every $\varepsilon>0$; no division by a zero range is needed.
